title: Ted Lewis and imitation New Orleans bands
summary: Hardy heard Ted Lewis but did not find New Orleans character in it, unlike Bob Crosby's band.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Uh-huh. Uh, after the success of the original Dixieland jazz band, there were several bands that represented themselves. As, uh, the original Dixieland jazz band. Well, not necessarily using the name, because maybe that was protected legally, I'm not sure. But, uh, there were several that represented themselves as being New Orleans-style bands. Uh-huh. Did you have a chance to hear anybody like Ted Lewis, or, uh...
Oh, yes, I've heard Ted Lewis in the past.
Or emphasize in the same period?
Yes, I think I did. I think I did. If it wasn't, if it wasn't before we went over, shortly after we came back, I heard Ted Lewis.
Uh, was there anything of New Orleans structure in there?

I didn't think so. I really didn't. There wasn't, it didn't have, there's a certain something that a band has to have to register with you, from the standpoint of associating it with New Orleans music. Now, Bob Crosby's band had it, in no uncertain terms. He had it. Dre Badouk, the drummer, you know, and some of the other boys that played in that band were recognized to be, uh, imbued with that, uh, uh, New Orleans's touch, if you know what I mean.
